blocks.text: 1. Reinforcement Learning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442849124-530871264.png

Supervised, Unsupervised, and Semi-Supervised Learning, the three previous topics, are all built around a fixed dataset that already exists before training even begins. Reinforcement Learning works in a genuinely different way: there is no fixed dataset of examples at all.

Instead, an agent takes actions within an environment, and learns purely from the feedback those actions actually produce over time. This is learning through trial, error, and reward, rather than learning from any labeled example, a fundamentally different setup from every other type covered so far in this module.
2. Core Vocabulary
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442849126-468063635.png

Reinforcement Learning introduces its own core vocabulary. The agent is the learner, the thing actually making decisions, and the environment is everything the agent interacts with, including anything that responds to the agent's choices in some way.

An action is a choice the agent actually makes at a given moment, a reward is feedback signaling how good, or how bad, that particular action turned out to be, and a state is the current situation the agent finds itself in at any given point. These five terms, agent, environment, action, reward, and state, get used constantly throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 3. The Feedback Loop
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442849126-343215186.png

Reinforcement Learning follows a continuously repeating feedback loop. The agent observes its current state, then chooses an action based on whatever it has already learned up to that point, using the vocabulary already introduced in the previous section.

The environment responds with a new state and a reward reflecting how good that chosen action actually was, and the agent updates what it has learned using that reward as direct feedback. This loop then repeats continuously, with the agent's decisions gradually improving as it accumulates more and more experience over time.
4. A Genuinely Distinctive Challenge: Delayed Reward

blocks.alt: A Genuinely Distinctive Challenge: Delayed Reward
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442849127-288098385.png

A genuinely distinctive challenge in Reinforcement Learning is delayed reward, where a single action's true value may not become clear until considerably later. A particular chess move, for instance, might only actually pay off ten moves further into the game, long after that specific move was actually made.

The agent must learn to credit earlier actions for later outcomes, a genuinely hard problem called credit assignment, figuring out which of many earlier actions actually deserves credit, or blame, for a reward that only arrived much later. This challenge simply does not exist in Supervised Learning, where feedback on a prediction arrives immediately and directly.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Credit assignment is one of the genuinely hardest, most actively researched problems in Reinforcement Learning. Even sophisticated modern systems still struggle with correctly crediting distant, indirect causes of a later reward.

blocks.text: 5. Exploration Versus Exploitation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442849127-859287473.png

A core tension every Reinforcement Learning agent genuinely faces is choosing between exploitation, repeating the action already known to work reasonably well, and exploration, trying something new and currently unproven instead.

Exploitation is safe, but it may miss a genuinely better, still-undiscovered option the agent simply has not tried yet. Exploration is riskier in the short term, since an untried action might turn out worse than what is already known, but it holds the potential of finding something considerably better than anything the agent has settled on so far.
6. Reward Versus a Labeled Correct Answer

blocks.alt: Reward Versus a Labeled Correct Answer
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442849127-937779830.png

This connects back to the correct-answer requirement already covered throughout the Supervised Learning topic. Supervised Learning tells a model the exact correct answer for every single training example, a considerably more direct, complete kind of feedback.

Reinforcement Learning instead tells an agent only how good a particular action turned out to be, never revealing the single best possible action it could have taken instead. This is a considerably sparser, more indirect kind of feedback, one of the genuine reasons Reinforcement Learning is often a harder learning problem than standard Supervised Learning.
7. Familiar, Real-World Examples

Reinforcement Learning already shows up in genuinely well-known systems. A game-playing agent mastering a board game purely through repeated self-play is a classic, widely recognized example, since no human ever actually labeled the single correct move for any given board position.

A robot learning to walk through repeated physical trial and error is another classic example, rewarded directly for forward progress and penalized for falling, gradually refining its own movements purely through this accumulated feedback over many, many attempts.
8. When Reinforcement Learning Is Genuinely the Right Fit

blocks.alt: When Reinforcement Learning Is Genuinely the Right Fit
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442849128-162006856.png

Reinforcement Learning is genuinely the right fit when the actual problem is a sequence of decisions, rather than one single prediction, playing an entire game from start to finish for instance, rather than simply classifying one single, isolated image.

It also fits well when a simulator, or a genuinely safe real environment, exists for actual trial and error to happen in. Without some safe way to practice, learning purely through real mistakes can be genuinely costly, or even outright dangerous, depending on exactly what the agent is actually being trained to do.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This is precisely why so much Reinforcement Learning research happens inside simulated environments, video games, physics simulators, rather than directly in the real world, where genuine trial and error would often be prohibitively expensive or risky.

blocks.text: 9. Closing the Four Major Types

This topic closes out the four major types of Machine Learning introduced across this topic and the three that came before it. Supervised Learning learns from labeled examples where the correct answer is already known, and Unsupervised Learning finds structure in data with no labels provided at all.

Semi-Supervised Learning combines a small labeled set with a much larger unlabeled pool, and Reinforcement Learning, covered here, learns through trial, error, and reward rather than through any fixed dataset. Together, these four types cover the vast majority of real-world Machine Learning problems this course goes on to explore in the modules ahead.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below implements a minimal Reinforcement Learning setup, an agent learning through repeated trial and error which of two actions produces a better reward.

code.content:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)

true_reward_probabilities = {"action_a": 0.3, "action_b": 0.7}  # unknown to the agent at the start
action_values = {"action_a": 0.5, "action_b": 0.5}  # the agent's initial, uninformed estimate
action_counts = {"action_a": 0, "action_b": 0}

for episode in range(200):
    if rng.rand() < 0.1:  # exploration: try a random action
        chosen_action = rng.choice(["action_a", "action_b"])
    else:  # exploitation: pick the action currently believed to be best
        chosen_action = max(action_values, key=action_values.get)

    reward = 1 if rng.rand() < true_reward_probabilities[chosen_action] else 0

    action_counts[chosen_action] += 1
    action_values[chosen_action] += (reward - action_values[chosen_action]) / action_counts[chosen_action]

print(f"After 200 episodes of trial and error:")
print(f"  Learned value of action_a: {action_values['action_a']:.3f} (chosen {action_counts['action_a']} times)")
print(f"  Learned value of action_b: {action_values['action_b']:.3f} (chosen {action_counts['action_b']} times)")
print("\nNo one told the agent which action was better, it discovered this purely through trial, error, and reward")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example directly demonstrates the exploration-versus-exploitation tension covered earlier in this topic: 10 percent of the time the agent explores randomly, and the rest of the time it exploits its current best estimate.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Reinforcement Learning has no fixed dataset; an agent learns purely from the feedback its actions produce.
Core vocabulary: agent, environment, action, reward, and state.
The feedback loop repeats continuously: observe state, choose action, receive reward, update, and repeat.
Delayed reward creates the genuinely hard credit assignment problem, crediting earlier actions for later outcomes.
Exploration versus exploitation is a core tension: trying something new versus repeating a known-good action.
Reward reveals only how good an action was, never the single best possible action, a sparser feedback than a label.
Game-playing agents mastering play through self-play, and robots learning to walk, are classic real-world examples.
Reinforcement Learning fits sequential decision problems with a safe simulator or environment for genuine trial and error.
This closes the four major types of Machine Learning; next up: preparing and understanding the data every model depends on.
